questions.text:
Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per
track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard
disk is ____
questions.solution:
Capacity = cylinders [latex]\times[/latex] surfaces [latex]\times[/latex] sectors per track [latex]\times[/latex] bytes per sector.

[latex]512\text{ GB}=2^{39}[/latex], 32 surfaces [latex]=2^5[/latex], 4096 sectors [latex]=2^{12}[/latex], 1024 bytes [latex]=2^{10}[/latex].

Cylinders [latex]=\dfrac{2^{39}}{2^5\times2^{12}\times2^{10}}=2^{12}=4096[/latex]

Answer: 4096

questions.text:
Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the
write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use
the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is
connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- WBC read miss: the LRU victim may be dirty and then it must be written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE ("never" is wrong).
- WTC read miss: with write-through, memory is always up to date, so a victim never needs to be written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- WBC write hit: the block becomes dirty, so the dirty bit can change from 0 to 1 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- WTC write miss: the victim block is never dirty, so it is never written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block

A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to
main memory
A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block

A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory
before loading the missed block to the cache

questions.text: Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: this is exactly the definition of forwarding (bypassing) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: a value available at the output of MEM (e.g. a loaded value) can be fed to the EX input of a later instruction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 3: forwarding cannot remove every stall. Example: load followed immediately by an instruction using the loaded value still needs 1 stall (load-use hazard) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 4: forwarding needs extra hardware (extra paths, multiplexers, hazard detection logic) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options:
In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an
earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction

In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the
input of the EX stage of the next instruction
Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls

Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the
pipeline stages

questions.text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Cycle stealing: DMA takes one bus cycle and moves one word [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Burst mode keeps the bus for the whole block (no repeated bus requests), so it has higher throughput for bulk transfer [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt-driven I/O [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. In programmed I/O the CPU keeps polling the device status and wastes cycles; interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device interrupts.
- Vectored interrupts give the ISR address directly (no polling to find the device), so ISR starts faster [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt driven I/O (FALSE)

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options:
In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O
device and main memory in a stolen cycle

For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the
cycle stealing mode

Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU utilization than the interrupt driven
I/O mechanism

The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored
interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts

questions.text:
An 8-way set associative cache of size 64 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) is used in a system with 32-bit address. The address is sub-divided into TAG, INDEX, and BLOCK OFFSET.
The number of bits in the TAG is ____.
questions.solution:
Size of one way [latex]=\frac{64\text{ KB}}{8}=8\text{ KB}=2^{13}[/latex] bytes.

INDEX + OFFSET bits together address one way, so they total 13 bits (the block size does not matter).

TAG [latex]=32-13=19[/latex] bits

Answer: 19
